summary:
"Turn back now: 170 minutes of oxygen left, base is 149 minutes away."

That is our EVA Copilot catching the point of no return in a demo on simulated suit telemetry: 170 looks like enough, but not with a safety reserve. Apollo's rule: never go farther than you can walk home. Martian Map helps astronauts apply it on Mars, on real terrain.

Pick a science target at Mount Sharp in Gale crater, Curiosity's home, and get one answer: GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, with reasons. It weighs the round trip in oxygen and time, an assumed 30-minute reserve, slopes a suited astronaut can walk, and the surface conditions of the chosen sol. Walk-back rings show how far from base is safe; real Curiosity photos preview each target.

A straight line looks shorter, yet in 17 of 28 target pairs it crosses terrain steeper than 20°. Our planner finds a safe route around it.

NASA and USGS data throughout (HiRISE, CTX, THEMIS, Curiosity REMS and RAD). Our elevation map matches Curiosity's own traverse, 95% within 1 m over 11,735 points. Speed and oxygen are estimates; rocks and sand are not modelled.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Martian Map is a 3D EVA (spacewalk) planner for Gale crater, Curiosity's home. The user picks a science target at Mount Sharp, or clicks any two points, and gets a walking route over real terrain plus one clear verdict: GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, with reasons. The route avoids slopes a suited astronaut cannot walk and prefers ground Curiosity has already driven. The verdict weighs the whole round trip in oxygen and time, a 30-minute emergency reserve (an assumption we state openly), the steepness of the way, and the surface conditions of the chosen Martian day (sol): temperature, pressure, UV and radiation. Walk-back rings show how far from base it is still safe to go. Target cards show real Curiosity photos, so the crew knows what to expect on arrival. An EVA Copilot demo then follows a walk and calls TURN BACK at the point of no return (it runs on simulated suit telemetry over real terrain).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

A map says where things are. A crew needs to know whether it can reach a place and return alive. Martian Map turns layered NASA data into that decision. In our tests a straight line crosses terrain steeper than 20° in 17 of 28 target pairs; the planner finds a safe route instead. We see it as a planning and training aid for mission planners, crew trainers and students, and as a first step toward tools that stay beside the crew during the walk.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Zustand and CesiumJS for the 3D globe. Backend: Python with FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image and Rasterio for terrain, slope, least-cost routing and oxygen metrics; pytest for tests. No special hardware: it runs in a web browser. A built-in offline mode shows precomputed routes if the server sleeps.

Data: USGS MSL Gale elevation map (HiRISE, CTX and HRSC tied to MOLA), Mars Trek imagery (HiRISE, CTX, Viking, THEMIS, MOLA, USGS geology), Curiosity REMS weather, RAD radiation, Curiosity traverse and NASA/JPL photos. Every source is listed in docs/sources.md.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It is a decision tool rather than another layer viewer. It brings the Apollo walkback rule (never go farther than you can walk home) to Mars on real terrain, and adds a Copilot that speaks up at the moment that matters.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Safety first: worst-case oxygen, a reserve, and uncertainty. Honesty: we checked our elevation map against Curiosity's own traverse (11,735 points, 95% within 1 m) and state the limits: speed and oxygen are estimates, rocks and sand are not modelled, weather is historical, and radiation is the mission average. We also considered usability, offline reliability, English-only materials and full source credits.
